---
name: batched-rows-need-distinct-conversations
description: "Pricing a multi-row decode pass on one sequence's tokens (or a fixed token per row) understates the MoE; three real conversations touch 26.8 experts a layer and cost 64 ms, not 52."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: d0d0daa2-ca18-4cc0-a764-84e089efc230
  modified: 2026-09-23T11:35:30.496Z
---

**2026-09-23, CONCURRENCY.md C5.** C5a priced a three-row pass with
`cmd/llm -graph -tokens 1,2,3`: **52 ms, 1.78 steps**. Those three rows are
three *consecutive tokens of one sequence*, which share experts. The server's
three concurrent agents ran **64 ms a pass**. `cmd/llm -batch` (one slot a
row, each prefilled with different wikitext) reproduced the 64 ms only once
it decoded greedily. Feeding each row a fixed token also read ~54 ms, because
a row that repeats its token reads the same experts every step. Three real
conversations touch **26.8 distinct experts a layer** against 10 for one row,
and the MoE is the part of a pass that grows with rows.

**Why:** a batched pass costs the *union* of its rows' experts, and anything
that correlates the rows' tokens shrinks the union.

**How to apply:** price batched decode with `cmd/llm -batch 1,2,3
-batch-depth 7000` (greedy, different text per slot), and check
`PassExperts` on the printed "distinct experts" line (~10/19/27 at 1/2/3
rows). The same trap applies to any rows-vs-cost claim about the MoE,
including P5's speculative verification rows, which *are* one sequence and
so priced correctly there. See [[concurrency-loadgen-run]] and
[[two-row-regime-needs-a-graph-gate]].
---
name: llm-resident-run
description: The whole-model runs (`cmd/llm -resident`, `-graph`, `-gen`, `-ppl`, `cmd/serve -llm`, `TestGraphLogits`) stage 82-83 GB of qwen3.8-flash-next; what they cost in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside them.
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Since L8a/L8b the dense banks are int8 rather than halves and residency is
81.89 GB with the head** (`-dense` 4.32 GB); `LLM_DENSE_FP16=1` puts every
block back on the old halves and restores the old sizes exactly, which is how
the two are compared. **A decode token is 31.7 ms and residency 79.85 GB as of
L8c-7 (2026-09-17)** with all five 4.5-bit families named in
`LLM_DENSE_BANK` — 40.5 ms at L8e, 33.3 at L8c-6, ~134 before L7d — so `-n 64`
is a ~2.0 s tail on top of staging. Without `LLM_DENSE_BANK` the run is still
L8a's int8 bank at 81.89 GB and 40.5 ms.

**Do not schedule a whole-model run above ~2560 rows**: at 48 layers
`-graph -tokens 3072` (or `-ppl -ctx 4096`) **never returns** — it stalls
inside the driver's submit with one host thread at 100% and the GPU at 2-3%,
and the shim's 20 s fence timeout never fires, so it hangs indefinitely rather
than erroring. 2048 and 2560 are fine; the 4-layer prefix is fine at 4096.
This is a known open question in `research/llm-vertical.md`, not a mistake to re-discover.

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, research/llm-vertical.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers (82.40 since L8a), ~35 s wall
clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is

chunks is ~15 s after staging) but **only screens for broken**: four chunks

name: ai-service-user-unit
description: "The ai server runs as a --user systemd unit on :11434; logs are journalctl --user -u ai, deploy.sh installs it, startup takes ~25 s, and it is deliberately served open with -token=."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
---

The `serve` binary runs as a **user** systemd unit, not a system one, and not
in the foreground:

- **Install/redeploy: `./deploy.sh`.** It builds `./ai` from `./cmd/serve`,
  substitutes the unit's `###` placeholder with `$(pwd)`, writes
  `~/.config/systemd/user/ai.service`, `daemon-reload`s and restarts.
  `./ai.service` in the repo is a *template*, not a script — running it gives
  `Permission denied`, which is the expected outcome, not a bug to fix.
- **`deploy.sh` ends with `journalctl --user -n 100 -f -u ai`,** which never
  returns. In an agent session run its steps by hand and skip the tail.
- **Logs: `journalctl --user -u ai`** (`--user` is required; it is invisible to
  the system journal). The server logs one line per backend at startup and
  `listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434` when all of them are up.
- **Startup is ~25 s** and ~13 GB peak, nearly all of it the Z-Image backend;
  tts/stt/embed land in the first 3 s. Don't conclude anything from the log
  before the image line.
- **State without tailing:**
  `systemctl --user show ai.service -p ActiveState -p SubState -p NRestarts`.
  The unit ships `Restart=always` + `RestartSec=1`, and the server `log.Fatal`s
  on any bad flag or missing checkpoint, so a config mistake becomes a silent
  ~26 s crash loop. A non-zero `NRestarts` (or "restart counter is at N" in the
  journal) is the tell; `systemctl --user reset-failed ai.service` before a
  fixed redeploy so the count reads clean.
- **Auth: omitting `-token` does not disable it.** The flag *defaults* to a
  non-empty token (`defaultToken` in `cmd/serve/main.go`), so a unit that says
  nothing about tokens requires a bearer header on every `/v1` request. Only an
  explicitly empty `-token=` opens the server. This cost an afternoon once.
- **The deployed unit runs `-token=` on purpose**, chosen 2026-09-18: open, no
  bearer header, on `0.0.0.0:11434` so the second machine can reach it. Don't
  "fix" the empty token back to a default — it is the configuration that was
  asked for. See [[deployment-two-machines]].
- The unit is **`disabled`** as of 2026-09-18 — it does not come back on boot
  or login without `systemctl --user enable ai` and `loginctl enable-linger`.

Anchor journal reads to the *current* instance
(`journalctl --user -u ai --since "@$(date -d "$(systemctl --user show
ai.service -p ExecMainStartTimestamp --value)" +%s)"`). A plain `--since -2min`
still contains the previous instance's crash lines and will make an
until-loop fire on a failure that is already fixed — the same self-matching
trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]. See
[[deployment-two-machines]] for which box this is meant to run on and
[[gpu-debugging-access]] for when it hangs rather than exits.

**The LLM line (P18, 2026-09-22)** is `-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`: the full trained context, ~66 s and ~83 GB to come up. See [[llm-full-context-262k]].

name: llm-bench-needs-bank-cache
description: "Benchmarking cmd/llm on the shipped banks needs LLM_BANK_CACHE set by hand, or every process start re-fits the MoE bank for eight minutes on all 32 cores."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**`cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`; `cmd/llm` never does** (the comment at
`cmd/serve/main.go:177` says so outright). So a `cmd/llm` run launched with
`LLM_MOE_BANK` at the shipped plan but no cache path re-fits `ffn_down_exps`
to IQ4_NL from scratch: 40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search,
`parallelFor` across every core. Measured 2026-09-19: **31 of 32 cores pinned
flat for the whole fit, 5731 CPU-seconds in the first 200 s, sys time 9.3 s**
— all arithmetic, no I/O. research/llm-vertical.md D21 prices the whole fit at ~8 minutes.

Set it and staging is a disk read instead:

    LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache

With it, a 48-layer stage at 131k cells was **58.5 s total, MoE block 19.4 s**,
71.01 GB of weights + 5.09 GB of arenas. The cache directory is 26 GB and was
already complete for the shipped plan (48/48 files per family). It is keyed on
(tensor, shape, source type, target type, arm, version) and lives inside the
checkpoint's directory — it does **not** hash the source bytes.

**The dense bank has no cache at all** (`llm/bank_q4.go`), so it re-fits every
start no matter what. Measured on the same 16 dense layers: banks off **8.6 s
wall / 46.9 CPU-s**, dense bank on **17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s** — 2.9x the CPU.
That part is unavoidable today.

**Why:** the CPU storm looks alarming and looks like inference gone wrong — it
is neither. It is startup-only weight preparation, which is why the served API
never shows it: the server pays the fit once ever and then holds the model
resident. During real inference the GPU sits at 98-99% and host cost is ~3 ms
of a ~31 ms token.

**How to apply:** set `LLM_BANK_CACHE` in every `cmd/llm` invocation that also
sets `LLM_MOE_BANK`, and budget ~60 s of staging rather than ~8 minutes. See
[[llm-resident-run]] and [[strix-halo-bench-runs]].
---
name: never-edit-source-during-a-sweep
description: "`go run` rebuilds on every invocation, so editing repo source while a multi-arm benchmark script is running kills every arm after the one already in flight."
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

**2026-09-21.** A four-arm 48-layer depth sweep lost three of its four arms.
The script called `go run ./cmd/llm` once per arm; arm 1 had already built and
ran fine; while it ran I edited `shaders/shaders.go` to add a new `//go:embed`
for a `.spv` that did not exist yet, and arms 2-4 each died instantly with

    shaders/shaders.go:2646:12: pattern llm_attn_expand.spv: no matching files found

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench
./cmd/llm` **once at the top** and run that binary for every arm. Then the
tree is free to edit while it runs, and every arm is provably the same build.
Select arms with environment variables read at dispatch time (this is what
`LLM_ATTN_SPLITS` and `LLM_ATTN_CELL_SPLITS` are for), never by rebuilding.

name: auto-committer-owns-main
description: "An external process auto-commits the strix-halo-vulkan working tree to main every ~30-45 min with the message \"ai\", and other sessions edit the same tree concurrently, so `go build ./...` can fail on someone else's half-written file."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 8382387e-ec90-4d7d-8642-1d65b8bbd10a
  modified: 2026-09-17T23:25:30.192Z
---

In `~/repos/strix-halo-vulkan` something outside the session commits the whole
working tree to `main` on a timer — the message is always `ai`, and the commits
land roughly every 30-45 minutes (observed 18:53, 19:37, 21:02, 21:36 on
2026-09-14). So a `git add -A && git commit` at the end of a session will often
print **"nothing to commit, working tree clean"** even though the work is
unsaved-looking: check `git show --stat HEAD` before concluding anything was
lost. There is an `origin` (github.com:theninj4/strix-halo-vulkan) but `main`
has **no upstream**, so nothing is pushed.

**Other sessions edit this tree at the same time.** On 2026-09-18 a second
session was mid-refactor in `zimage/pipeline` and mid-write in `api/images.go`
while this one built `embed/`: `go build ./...` failed twice on *their*
undefined symbols (`p.latentH`, `formatSize`), minutes apart, and both cleared
on their own. Check `git status --short` and file mtimes before believing a
build break is yours, and build the packages you touched
(`go build ./embed/ ./api/ …`) rather than `./...` while it lasts.

**Why:** the commit log is therefore not the project's narrative — `TODO.md`
is, and every session appends a handoff to it. That is why the repo's own docs
say to read `TODO.md`/the current vertical file first.

**How to apply:** don't branch before committing here (the whole history is
direct-to-main), don't amend the `ai` commits to "improve" them, and put the
session's story in `TODO.md` rather than in a commit message. Edit files with
targeted replacements rather than whole-file rewrites when another session may
be in the same file, and never "fix" a symbol that belongs to their in-flight
work. See [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] and [[phase-2-pivot-to-pipeline]] for what
the docs expect a session to record.

name: batched-rows-need-distinct-conversations
description: "Pricing a multi-row decode pass on one sequence's tokens (or a fixed token per row) understates the MoE; three real conversations touch 26.8 experts a layer and cost 64 ms, not 52."
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: d0d0daa2-ca18-4cc0-a764-84e089efc230
  modified: 2026-09-23T11:35:30.496Z
---

**2026-09-23, CONCURRENCY.md C5.** C5a priced a three-row pass with
`cmd/llm -graph -tokens 1,2,3`: **52 ms, 1.78 steps**. Those three rows are
three *consecutive tokens of one sequence*, which share experts. The server's
three concurrent agents ran **64 ms a pass**. `cmd/llm -batch` (one slot a
row, each prefilled with different wikitext) reproduced the 64 ms only once
it decoded greedily. Feeding each row a fixed token also read ~54 ms, because
a row that repeats its token reads the same experts every step. Three real
conversations touch **26.8 distinct experts a layer** against 10 for one row,
and the MoE is the part of a pass that grows with rows.

**Why:** a batched pass costs the *union* of its rows' experts, and anything
that correlates the rows' tokens shrinks the union.

**How to apply:** price batched decode with `cmd/llm -batch 1,2,3
-batch-depth 7000` (greedy, different text per slot), and check
`PassExperts` on the printed "distinct experts" line (~10/19/27 at 1/2/3
rows). The same trap applies to any rows-vs-cost claim about the MoE,
including P5's speculative verification rows, which *are* one sequence and
so priced correctly there. See [[concurrency-loadgen-run]] and
[[two-row-regime-needs-a-graph-gate]].

  `listening on http://0.0.0.0:11434` when all of them are up.
- **Startup is ~25 s** and ~13 GB peak, nearly all of it the Z-Image backend;
  tts/stt/embed land in the first 3 s. Don't conclude anything from the log
  before the image line.
- **State without tailing:**
  `systemctl --user show ai.service -p ActiveState -p SubState -p NRestarts`.
  The unit ships `Restart=always` + `RestartSec=1`, and the server `log.Fatal`s
  on any bad flag or missing checkpoint, so a config mistake becomes a silent
  ~26 s crash loop. A non-zero `NRestarts` (or "restart counter is at N" in the
  journal) is the tell; `systemctl --user reset-failed ai.service` before a
  fixed redeploy so the count reads clean.
- **Auth: omitting `-token` does not disable it.** The flag *defaults* to a
  non-empty token (`defaultToken` in `cmd/serve/main.go`), so a unit that says
  nothing about tokens requires a bearer header on every `/v1` request. Only an
  explicitly empty `-token=` opens the server. This cost an afternoon once.
- **The deployed unit runs `-token=` on purpose**, chosen 2026-09-18: open, no
  bearer header, on `0.0.0.0:11434` so the second machine can reach it. Don't
  "fix" the empty token back to a default — it is the configuration that was
  asked for. See [[deployment-two-machines]].
- The unit is **`disabled`** as of 2026-09-18 — it does not come back on boot
  or login without `systemctl --user enable ai` and `loginctl enable-linger`.

Anchor journal reads to the *current* instance
(`journalctl --user -u ai --since "@$(date -d "$(systemctl --user show
ai.service -p ExecMainStartTimestamp --value)" +%s)"`). A plain `--since -2min`
still contains the previous instance's crash lines and will make an
until-loop fire on a failure that is already fixed — the same self-matching
trap as [[watch-loops-must-not-match-themselves]]. See
[[deployment-two-machines]] for which box this is meant to run on and
[[gpu-debugging-access]] for when it hangs rather than exits.

**The LLM line (P18, 2026-09-22)** is `-llm -llm-ctx 262144 -llm-batch 8192`: the full trained context, ~66 s and ~83 GB to come up. See [[llm-full-context-262k]].
---
name: llm-bench-needs-bank-cache
description: "Benchmarking cmd/llm on the shipped banks needs LLM_BANK_CACHE set by hand, or every process start re-fits the MoE bank for eight minutes on all 32 cores."
metadata:
  type: project
---

**`cmd/serve` sets `LLM_BANK_CACHE`; `cmd/llm` never does** (the comment at
`cmd/serve/main.go:177` says so outright). So a `cmd/llm` run launched with
`LLM_MOE_BANK` at the shipped plan but no cache path re-fits `ffn_down_exps`
to IQ4_NL from scratch: 40 billion weights through a sixteen-scale search,
`parallelFor` across every core. Measured 2026-09-19: **31 of 32 cores pinned
flat for the whole fit, 5731 CPU-seconds in the first 200 s, sys time 9.3 s**
— all arithmetic, no I/O. research/llm-vertical.md D21 prices the whole fit at ~8 minutes.

Set it and staging is a disk read instead:

    LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache

With it, a 48-layer stage at 131k cells was **58.5 s total, MoE block 19.4 s**,
71.01 GB of weights + 5.09 GB of arenas. The cache directory is 26 GB and was
already complete for the shipped plan (48/48 files per family). It is keyed on
(tensor, shape, source type, target type, arm, version) and lives inside the
checkpoint's directory — it does **not** hash the source bytes.

**The dense bank has no cache at all** (`llm/bank_q4.go`), so it re-fits every
start no matter what. Measured on the same 16 dense layers: banks off **8.6 s
wall / 46.9 CPU-s**, dense bank on **17.4 s / 134.6 CPU-s** — 2.9x the CPU.
That part is unavoidable today.

**Why:** the CPU storm looks alarming and looks like inference gone wrong — it
is neither. It is startup-only weight preparation, which is why the served API
never shows it: the server pays the fit once ever and then holds the model
resident. During real inference the GPU sits at 98-99% and host cost is ~3 ms
of a ~31 ms token.

**How to apply:** set `LLM_BANK_CACHE` in every `cmd/llm` invocation that also
sets `LLM_MOE_BANK`, and budget ~60 s of staging rather than ~8 minutes. See
[[llm-resident-run]] and [[strix-halo-bench-runs]].
---
name: never-edit-source-during-a-sweep
description: "`go run` rebuilds on every invocation, so editing repo source while a multi-arm benchmark script is running kills every arm after the one already in flight."
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

**2026-09-21.** A four-arm 48-layer depth sweep lost three of its four arms.
The script called `go run ./cmd/llm` once per arm; arm 1 had already built and
ran fine; while it ran I edited `shaders/shaders.go` to add a new `//go:embed`
for a `.spv` that did not exist yet, and arms 2-4 each died instantly with

    shaders/shaders.go:2646:12: pattern llm_attn_expand.spv: no matching files found

~25 minutes of measurement, and the failure was silent in the sweep's own log
until the end.

[[strix-halo-bench-runs]] already says "edit *text* while it runs, nothing
else" — that rule is about CPU contention perturbing the numbers. This is a
second, harder reason: **a multi-arm script that invokes `go run` rebuilds the
tree at the start of every arm**, so the source it compiles is whatever the
tree holds *then*, not what it held at launch. Even an edit that compiles
would silently measure a different binary in later arms, which is worse than
a crash.

**How to apply:** make the benchmark script `go build -o <scratchpad>/bench
./cmd/llm` **once at the top** and run that binary for every arm. Then the
tree is free to edit while it runs, and every arm is provably the same build.
Select arms with environment variables read at dispatch time (this is what
`LLM_ATTN_SPLITS` and `LLM_ATTN_CELL_SPLITS` are for), never by rebuilding.
---
name: auto-committer-owns-main
description: "An external process auto-commits the strix-halo-vulkan working tree to main every ~30-45 min with the message \"ai\", and other sessions edit the same tree concurrently, so `go build ./...` can fail on someone else's half-written file."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 8382387e-ec90-4d7d-8642-1d65b8bbd10a
  modified: 2026-09-17T23:25:30.192Z
---

In `~/repos/strix-halo-vulkan` something outside the session commits the whole
working tree to `main` on a timer — the message is always `ai`, and the commits
land roughly every 30-45 minutes (observed 18:53, 19:37, 21:02, 21:36 on
2026-09-14). So a `git add -A && git commit` at the end of a session will often
print **"nothing to commit, working tree clean"** even though the work is
unsaved-looking: check `git show --stat HEAD` before concluding anything was
lost. There is an `origin` (github.com:theninj4/strix-halo-vulkan) but `main`
has **no upstream**, so nothing is pushed.

**Other sessions edit this tree at the same time.** On 2026-09-18 a second
session was mid-refactor in `zimage/pipeline` and mid-write in `api/images.go`
while this one built `embed/`: `go build ./...` failed twice on *their*
undefined symbols (`p.latentH`, `formatSize`), minutes apart, and both cleared
on their own. Check `git status --short` and file mtimes before believing a
build break is yours, and build the packages you touched
(`go build ./embed/ ./api/ …`) rather than `./...` while it lasts.

**Why:** the commit log is therefore not the project's narrative — `TODO.md`
is, and every session appends a handoff to it. That is why the repo's own docs
say to read `TODO.md`/the current vertical file first.

**How to apply:** don't branch before committing here (the whole history is
direct-to-main), don't amend the `ai` commits to "improve" them, and put the
session's story in `TODO.md` rather than in a commit message. Edit files with
targeted replacements rather than whole-file rewrites when another session may
be in the same file, and never "fix" a symbol that belongs to their in-flight
work. See [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] and [[phase-2-pivot-to-pipeline]] for what
the docs expect a session to record.

research/llm-vertical.md:714:| ~~**P5**~~ | ~~**MTP speculation**~~ — **done 2026-09-19, and it closes as a measured loss: lossless, and 0.98x.** P5c built the rollback and the loop and the stage's own gate holds — `result_norm` identical to the last place through rejected passes against a control that moves it by rms 8.5e-01, and the loop's ids identical to the plain loop's at ctx 512 and at 2048 cells with a 1024-token prompt. **34.65 against 36.38 tok/s and 28.20 against 31.56**, two runs each on the shipped banks (0.98x/0.98x on the checkpoint's own widths — narrowing the trunk makes speculation *worse*, because the draft head does not narrow with it and acceptance falls). The gap to 1.33x is three numbers and none is the rollback: the verification pass is **1.32 steps, not P5b's 24-layer 1.17** (at 48 layers the M-independent head, PLE and host are 13% of a step rather than 24%); acceptance on generated prose is **64.1%, not 74.0%**; and the round is a **two-state chain**, because at R = 2 a rejection's re-run prefix fills the pass and displaces the draft — `(pass + draft) + (1−a)·pass` for exactly two tokens, which the design priced as free at general M. **Two of the design's rollback entries were wrong in the cheap direction**: the deferred ring write is *impossible* (`aQKV` is one arena shared by 36 layers, so a pass ends holding layer 47's projection and there is nothing to re-issue the others from — the rings ping-pong instead), and the pooled indexer table does *not* self-heal (a block is written the one time a run completes its cells and never again, so `Rewind` snapshots it). **Three defects in P5b**, two silent: `PinSchedule` stopped pinning at two rows, the four MoE expert dispatches never named their R-row pipeline (a 45x error on the residual, invisible to a block test whose control is a control on the *combine*), and the R-row GEMV re-read the bank per row (`moe.up` at **101 GB/s against 141**), worth **0.91x → 0.98x**. Every block but the MoE takes one step up at M = 2 and is then **flat to M = 8** on identical weight bytes — `hc` 2.1 → 13.9 → 13.8 ms, `dn` 4.2 → 8.3 → 8.5, `attn` 1.2 → 2.7 → 2.7 — which is D15's refusal and nothing else; only the MoE keeps climbing, and that half is real (**10 experts at M = 1, 17 at 2, 36 at 4, 49 at 8** against a 1.327 GB routed row of D21's 4.132). **The rollback is the easy part**: 120.75 MB, of which the 113.25 MB of recurrent state **ping-pongs for nothing** (`llm_dn_scan.comp` loads S into registers once and stores it once) and the 7.5 MB of convolution rings is **deferred rather than copied** (`llm_seq_hist.comp` is one dispatch at the end of a block) — and a correctness finding beside it: **both rings are corrupted by a single rejected token**, silently, because a ring is addressed by absolute position modulo its length. **P5a** is the draft head as a *passive observer* — acceptance needs no rollback and no kernel — **P5b** the R-row decode kernels, **P5c** the loop. **P5b done 2026-09-19**: all four decode GEMVs carry **R rows per tile**, `ROWS` a specialization constant so the ~130 `.spv` of those families do not double, and a two-row whole-graph pass is **19.5 ms against 16.6 at one row — 1.17x against the 1.16x projected, where it was 54.1**; `hc` 13.9 → **2.0** ms, `moe` 25.5 → **8.2**, and three of the four blocks are *faster* at two rows than at one. One row unregressed. D15's refusal moved to `GEMVMaxRows` rather than going away. [Write-up](p5b-r-row-decode.md) | **P5a done 2026-09-19: `a₁ = 74.0%`** (1024 rounds, n_ctx 2048, teacher-forced, against a zeroed-hidden control at 9.8%), E[tokens] 1.74 at depth 1 to 3.02 at 6, **flat in context** and identical over two runs. research/README.md:111:| [P12](p12-prefill-round-two.md) | **Prefill round two: two bit-exact kernel changes, and four of P11's own leads measured away.** Prefill is **1.012-1.025x on both axes** — 1191.2 → **1207.7 tok/s** at 2048 rows, 1370.5 → **1403.9** at 8192 (**3.59x** llama.cpp), and 651.3 → **667.7** at 64 000 cells — with the two base passes agreeing to 1370.5/1370.5 and 651.3/651.2. Two changes hold. **The attention kernel's row max ran on sixteen lanes of sixty-four**: `for (i = lane; i < BM; i += WAVE)` with BM 16 and WAVE 64, KTIL times a block, two barriers and a store around each pass, each active lane then walking TILE cells serially with a `selected()` bit test. The whole key block is now staged at once (`stage` holds QT\*KTIL tiles, 2 KB of LDS) and RCL = WAVE/BM lanes share a row, folded by a **clustered subgroup max** — **bit-identical**, because a max has no rounding and the cells scanned are the same ones in the same order, and the wave is converged where the op is issued. **1.16x on the kernel at 512 tokens** and **+1.6-1.8% of a prefill token from 8000 cells on**. And **a K-quant block's header is one sixteen-byte load, not four dwords**: Q4_K/Q5_K open every block with `d`, `dmin` and twelve packed scale bytes, so at BK 32 a lane was issuing eight scalar loads a K-step against the nibbles' four `uvec4`s — L5b-7's rule for the third time. Every block of both formats is 16-byte aligned (region, row and block all multiples of 16) and `MoEGPU.build` now says so rather than trusting it; with the nibble extracted in two ops instead of four it is **`moe.up` 12 118 → 11 755 µs at 2048 tokens (1.031x)** with **`moe.down` (IQ4_NL, untouched) flat as the control**. **And four refusals, which close most of P11's open list.** **Both of `hc.cn`'s named suspects cost nothing**: deleting the 256-way reduction tree outright measures **5331.5 µs against 5325.8** — the eight barriers four times a token are **free**, so the non-bit-exact rewrite queued behind them would have bought zero — and replacing the per-token `gamma` read with a constant measures **5332.9**, because it is the same 40 KB every token and the MALL serves it. Its 57% of copy bandwidth is now unexplained *and* out of hypotheses. **The block skip hoisted out of the loop is 1.00x at every depth**: at 64k a query tile walks ~2000 blocks and skips ~1480, each paying a **dependent** global read, and a cost model where a dead block is ~20% of a live one reproduces `attn.attn`'s 9.8-against-16.0 TFLOP/s exactly — so the whole key range was voted on up front in one coalesced pass with a subgroup ballot, no atomics and no per-block barrier, and it bought **nothing**. The reason is the **exact converse of P8**: a decode step dispatches 24 single-wave workgroups and nothing hides a serial walk, but a 2048-token prefill dispatches **3072**, so that latency is already covered — *latency that matters at decode does not matter at prefill, because prefill has occupancy*. It is still live for decode, where it was deliberately never built. **The selection mask loop is 3.5-8%**, not the rest of the gap. **The MoE's per-element affine is a floor**: gutting the whole scale path is 1.21x at 2048 tokens, P12-2 takes the loads and integer ops out of that, and what remains — an int→float convert, an FMA and an f16 convert on every weight — has no bit-exact cheaper form, since packed fp16 costs thirteen bits of mantissa and `v_cvt_pkrtz` rounds the wrong way. **The ubatch remains the largest number on the board**: 2048 → 8192 is 1.16x and the curve has not flattened, which is a memory budget rather than a kernel. |
research/README.md:112:| [P11](p11-prefill.md) | **Prompt processing: the ubatch was the largest number in the file and the cheapest, and the MoE's row padding is not a cost at all.** `cmd/serve` prefilled in **512-token chunks** because that is llama.cpp's best ubatch and what every number in this vertical is quoted against — and 512 is the **worst rung this graph has**. llama.cpp plateaus at its ubatch; this one does not, because the MoE's arithmetic intensity is the **routing's**: at 512 tokens 274 of 512 experts are unpacked whole to serve 5120 rows, and the schedule pads those out to 11 904. `-llm-batch` is now **2048** — 1.12 GB of arenas for **1.64x** (667.4 → 1093.3 tok/s at 48 layers and ctx 4096; **667 → 1053 through HTTP** on a 4128-token prompt), where the 1.49 GB to 4096 buys 13% more. Separately, `llm_moe_gemm.comp`'s MODE 0 stages BM **scattered** rows of the block input into LDS per K-step, and it was doing it one half at a time: **32 two-byte loads a lane a K-step at BM 64**, against the eight the B unpack issues for four times the data. That is L5b-7's finding on the *operand* instead of the weight — the kernel is bound by how many load instructions it issues — so the halves arena is bound a second time as `uvec4` (binding 7) and a row is four aligned loads: **`moe.up` 14 918 → 11 936 µs a layer at 2048 tokens (1.25x)**, bit for bit the same slab, MODE 1 untouched as the control. The graph: **1079.6 → 1165.1 tok/s at 2048 rows, 1250.1 → 1328.5 at 8192 (3.40x llama.cpp)**, two runs agreeing to 0.2%. **Three changes that look right and are not**, all reverted, all one answer: a 16-row alignment with a row count per record (13.7 ms against 11.9 — the per-fragment branch inside the unrolled accumulator loops costs more than 35% of the rows, and the kernel goes to 256 VGPRs), three sub-lists one dispatch a rung (12.5 — no guard anywhere, but small grids do not fill the machine and three grids have three ramps), and a **128-row block** (13.5 — 608 tiles to 477 but the padding to 2.98x, because with 399 experts touched **the floor is one tile an expert** however wide the block). **At prefill this GEMM is bound by its per-tile slab unpack and the rows are very nearly free**; L5b built the padding as a cost to justify and it is not one, so the way in is fewer *tiles*, which is a bigger ubatch — which is the result. **A second round takes it to 3.51x.** `hc.cn` — the combine fused with the next mixer's norm, the second largest kernel in a prefill and one that does **no arithmetic** — was one workgroup per (token, stream), and the four streams of a token combine *the same* block output row: 110 KB a token where 80 would do. One workgroup a token, the output held in ten registers a thread already had spare, is **1.37-1.44x on the kernel** and bit-identical (each stream still reduces through the same 256-way tree), taking the graph to **1191.8 / 1372.2 tok/s** at 2048 / 8192 rows and 64k prefill to **654 tok/s** from 440. And `AttnGPU.SelSkip` measures, for the first time, **how much of the key axis the QSA selection actually lets the attention kernel skip**: at 64 000 cells the shipped 16x32 tile keeps **25.9%** of (query tile, key block) pairs live, a 16-cell tile would keep 18.5%, and a single query row 14.7% — so **a per-query gather is worth 1.76x, not the 31x the 3.2% density suggests**, which is L4b's "at prefill the density makes it pointless" with a number on it. The 1.40x between a 32-cell block and a 16-cell one was built as a bit-identical per-k-tile skip and is **1.18x slower** (866.1 → 737.2 tok/s at 16k), and at 64k slow enough to hold the ring past P0's two-second watchdog. Two kernels, one rule: **a branch inside an unrolled cooperative-matrix loop costs more than the work it removes** — neither kernel is arithmetic-bound, so change the loop's granularity, not what happens inside it. What is left of the depth term is that `attn.attn` does its useful work at **9.8 TFLOP/s at 64k against 16.0 at depth zero**, and the row max it only runs when the selection is on uses **sixteen of sixty-four lanes** |
research/README.md:115:| [P5c](p5c-speculative-loop.md) | **Speculation is built, lossless, and 0.95x.** The rollback as designed — the recurrent state and both convolution rings ping-ponged, `Commit`/`Rewind` — plus the loop, and both gates hold: `result_norm` **identical to the last place** through rejected passes against a control that moves it by rms 8.5e-01, and the loop's ids identical to the plain loop's token for token at ctx 512 and at 2048 cells with a 1024-token prompt. **34.65 against 36.38 tok/s and 28.20 against 31.56**, two runs each on the shipped banks. The gap to the projected 1.33x is three numbers and none is the rollback: the verification pass is **1.36 steps, not P5b's 24-layer 1.17**; acceptance is **65.6% on prose and 46.9% at a long context, not 74.0%**, against a break-even of ~0.72 — and **narrowing the trunk makes both worse**, since the draft head stages at the checkpoint's own widths and does not shrink with D19/D20/D21; and the round is a **two-state chain**, because at R = 2 a rejection's re-run prefix fills the pass and displaces the draft. **Two of the design's rollback entries were wrong in the cheap direction**: the deferred ring write is *impossible* (`aQKV` is one arena shared by 36 DeltaNet layers, so a pass ends holding layer 47's projection), and the pooled indexer table does *not* self-heal (a block is written the one time a run completes its cells and never again). **Three defects in P5b, two silent**: `PinSchedule` stopped pinning at two rows once P5b taught `MoEPlanFor` to name the GEMV there; the four MoE expert dispatches **never named their R-row pipeline**, so every two-row batch ran the one-row kernel (45x on the residual, invisible to a block test whose `rowMoved` control is a control on the *combine*); and the R-row GEMV **re-read the bank per row** — `moe.up` at 101 GB/s against 141 — because "it is in the L1 after the first pass" holds on a two-layer fixture and not across 48 layers of expert bank, worth **0.91x → 0.98x**. Plus **453 MB of host memset a pass** in `DeltaNetGPU.Resize`, which only a short *re-recorded* pass can see. Two rungs added to `TestGraphIsAChunkSplit` — **two tokens at a time and three** — because a two-row schedule was gated nowhere and all three defects are visible there. And two things nobody had priced: **speculation stops at 2048 cells** (`blk.48` states no compress ratio), and **a fresh sequence is not independent of the one before it** — three plain greedy runs over one prompt give three different texts, deterministically |
research/README.md:122:| [P1](p1-decode-attribution.md) | **The decode step, attributed to the dispatch: LLM2's "~12 ms unexplained" is 5.54 ms of weight-streaming dispatches below 227 GB/s, 3.46 ms of dispatches that stream no weight, and 3.01 ms of host.** The step sums to 30.52 ms with a 5 us residual over 36 dispatch labels and six host phases. **The n-gram gather was disk latency, and it was serial**: sixteen random rows of a 28.80 GB mmap'd table are **16.3 major faults a step**, served one at a time — issuing them concurrently leaves the fault count identical to two decimal places and is **7.0-7.5x** (853/819 us → 122/109), taking the gather 2.244 → 0.902 ms and decode **31.51 → 32.72 tok/s, 1.30x llama.cpp**. That is the other half of D9: `MADV_RANDOM` made each fault small, this stops them being serialised. Seven of eight weight-reading families measure 147-204 GB/s and **`hyper_conn` measures 114.6** — not bandwidth, since D14 says those weights never leave the MALL, but **485 dispatches a pass at 1.4-17 us each**: the block is 13.6% of the step for 8.4% of the bytes. `moe.down` is **147.5 GB/s against `moe.up`'s 200.6** off the same bank, a shape never re-screened (D11/D12). Idea 2's pre-recorded command buffer finally has a price — **1.96 ms, 6.4%, ~+2.2 tok/s** — and is the *fourth* item, not the first. **Idea 9 closed**: the 0.38 GB is the MoE router and the shared expert, which the inventory files as dense and the graph's table files with the MoE; every ceiling is now quoted on one basis, **4.281 GB a token** |

Its 57% of copy bandwidth is now unexplained *and* out of hypotheses. **The block skip hoisted out of the loop is 1.00x at every depth**: at 64k a query tile walks ~2000 blocks and skips ~1480, each paying a **dependent** global read, and a cost model where a dead block is ~20% of a live one reproduces `attn.attn`'s 9.8-against-16.0 TFLOP/s exactly — so the whole key range was voted on up front in one coalesced pass with a subgroup ballot, no atomics and no per-block barrier, and it bought **nothing**. The reason is the **exact converse of P8**: a decode step dispatches 24 single-wave workgroups and nothing hides a serial walk, but a 2048-token prefill dispatches **3072**, so that latency is already covered — *latency that matters at decode does not matter at prefill, because prefill has occupancy*. It is still live for decode, where it was deliberately never built. **The selection mask loop is 3.5-8%**, not the rest of the gap. **The MoE's per-element affine is a floor**: gutting the whole scale path is 1.21x at 2048 tokens, P12-2 takes the loads and integer ops out of that, and what remains — an int→float convert, an FMA and an f16 convert on every weight — has no bit-exact cheaper form, since packed fp16 costs thirteen bits of mantissa and `v_cvt_pkrtz` rounds the wrong way. **The ubatch remains the largest number on the board**: 2048 → 8192 is 1.16x and the curve has not flattened, which is a memory budget rather than a kernel. |
research/README.md:112:| [P11](p11-prefill.md) | **Prompt processing: the ubatch was the largest number in the file and the cheapest, and the MoE's row padding is not a cost at all.** `cmd/serve` prefilled in **512-token chunks** because that is llama.cpp's best ubatch and what every number in this vertical is quoted against — and 512 is the **worst rung this graph has**. llama.cpp plateaus at its ubatch; this one does not, because the MoE's arithmetic intensity is the **routing's**: at 512 tokens 274 of 512 experts are unpacked whole to serve 5120 rows, and the schedule pads those out to 11 904. `-llm-batch` is now **2048** — 1.12 GB of arenas for **1.64x** (667.4 → 1093.3 tok/s at 48 layers and ctx 4096; **667 → 1053 through HTTP** on a 4128-token prompt), where the 1.49 GB to 4096 buys 13% more. Separately, `llm_moe_gemm.comp`'s MODE 0 stages BM **scattered** rows of the block input into LDS per K-step, and it was doing it one half at a time: **32 two-byte loads a lane a K-step at BM 64**, against the eight the B unpack issues for four times the data. One workgroup a token, the output held in ten registers a thread already had spare, is **1.37-1.44x on the kernel** and bit-identical (each stream still reduces through the same 256-way tree), taking the graph to **1191.8 / 1372.2 tok/s** at 2048 / 8192 rows and 64k prefill to **654 tok/s** from 440. The 1.40x between a 32-cell block and a 16-cell one was built as a bit-identical per-k-tile skip and is **1.18x slower** (866.1 → 737.2 tok/s at 16k), and at 64k slow enough to hold the ring past P0's two-second watchdog. Two kernels, one rule: **a branch inside an unrolled cooperative-matrix loop costs more than the work it removes** — neither kernel is arithmetic-bound, so change the loop's granularity, not what happens inside it. What is left of the depth term is that `attn.attn` does its useful work at **9.8 TFLOP/s at 64k against 16.0 at depth zero**, and the row max it only runs when the selection is on uses **sixteen of sixty-four lanes** |

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

**`go test ./llm/` needs `-timeout 60m`.** Go's default is ten minutes and the
suite runs past it inside `TestQSASelectionSurvivesOurScores`. What you get is
a panic stack and `FAIL strix-halo-vulkan/llm 600.024s`, which **reads as a
real failure and is not one**. With a warm bank cache the whole suite is
~180 s; cold it is much longer.

**`TestGraphLogits` passes as of 2026-09-22** — it now takes a near-tie on
argmax (7 tokens, "The capital of France is Paris."). Its diagnostics at
f062e28 are `result_output ... maxAbs 1.987e+00 at 19208, rms 3.314e-01`,
argmax ours 11751 vs llama.cpp 561, "0.4920 apart" — P16's three changes
reproduce them byte for byte. (The older `2.507e+00 at 141557` digits are from
before the test changed.) To get a base to diff against, a `git worktree` of
HEAD needs `models/` and `reference/out/` symlinked in (both gitignored) and
the `.spv` files copied, or the test silently prints nothing.

**That identity is also the cheapest whole-model bit-exactness check there
is.** A change that claims to be bit-exact should reproduce those numbers to
the digit through all 48 layers — stronger than any block test, and it costs
one 61 s run.

**`LLM_BANK_CACHE` is a relative path, and `go test ./llm/` resolves it
against `llm/`.** So exporting the usual
`LLM_BANK_CACHE=models/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-GGUF/bank-cache` and running the
tests silently builds a **23 GB** duplicate at `llm/models/`, untracked. Use
an absolute path, or `rm -rf llm/models` afterwards. The real cache
(26 GB, 199 files) is at the repo root.

`go test ./llm/ -run 'TestAttn|TestMoEGPU|TestGraphIsAChunkSplit' -timeout 30m`
(~80 s), and run the full suite only when something broad moved. See

lines: +// TailRow copies out, for every staged layer, the pooled row of the block
+// that holds cell `past`, which is not whole yet and so still holds what a
+// fresh sequence filled it with: cell 0 pooled `ratio` times (blockRange).
+// ResetTail writes that row back over blocks [from/ratio, to/ratio] (C4).
+// **The tail score reads it.** llm_attn_score_wmma.comp scores block `nBid`,
+// the first that is not whole, from its pooled row, and every block past it
+// shares that one score. A continuation that ran from `from` to `to` and
+// was then abandoned completed the blocks in between with its own keys, and
+// nothing rewrites one until a later run completes it again, so a restored
+// sequence would score its partial block from a stranger's keys. The
+// selection survives that, but not bit for bit: the score is one term of
+// the sort that orders the blocks a query reads.

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='CONCURRENCY.md'
s=open(p).read()
section='''## The MoE GEMV's load count (done 2026-09-23)

**The expert GEMV issued one scalar load per four bytes of Q4_K nibbles,
plus four more for the block header, and it was bound by the load count.**
`moe.up` and `moe.down` run over the same tiles, but at three rows `moe.up`
streamed its Q4_K gate and up banks at ~128 GB/s while `moe.down` read its
IQ4_NL bank at ~190 (1.84 and 0.92 MB an expert). This is P12's finding
about the GEMM's slab, made again for `llm_moe_gemv.comp`, which never got
it. Two changes:

- **The load is outside the row loop.** `dotDword` had loaded, decoded and
  dotted one row, and the row loop called it once per row. So a tile with R
  real rows issued every load R times. The shared expert is the same bytes at
  any row count, and it showed this most clearly: `shexp.up` took 15.6 /
  23.4 / 32.2 µs a dispatch at 1/2/3 rows. Now `unpackDword` loads once and
  `dotRow` is the per-row half, and every product and sum stays in the order
  it had. Three rows: `shexp.up` 1.55 → 0.98 ms, `shexp.down` 0.73 → 0.54,
  and the pass 53.6 → 53.0 ms.
- **Q4_K is walked a quad at a time.** Four consecutive payload dwords are 16
  bytes of one 64-element group and share both scale pairs, so a quad is one
  `uvec4` header load plus one `uvec4` payload load, where the dword walk
  issued twenty scalar loads. Every Q4_K block is 16-byte aligned (P12
  checks it). The sum is now grouped by quad, so the decode path is **not**
  bit-identical to before. `TestMoEGPUDecode` still reads rms 2.54e-06
  against the GEMM, the batched-rows gate is still bit-identical row for
  row, and prefill (`TestGraphLogits`) is untouched to the digit.
- **The routed up mode moved from v64w4 to v16w4.** A row is 80 quads, which
  16 divides and 64 does not. L8e-2 once measured v16w4 42 ms worse in the
  whole model on the dword kernel, so the choice was made in the graph, not
  on the cache-hot block ladder: v16w4 < v32w4 < v64w4, two runs each. The
  shared expert's rung (v64w4) was within 0.04 ms of the alternatives and
  stays.

`cmd/llm -batch 1,2,3 -batch-depth 7000`, 48 layers, shipped banks; "after"
is four runs from two sweeps of the final configuration:

| rows | before | after | a row | aggregate | `moe.up` | `shexp.up` |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 29.2 ms | **27.6-27.7** | 34.2 → **36.2 tok/s** | | 6.02 → 4.60 | 0.75 → 0.72 |
| 2 | 42.5 | **39.0-40.0** | 23.5 → 25.3 | 47.1 → **50.6** | 12.6 → 10.0 | 1.12 → 0.92 |
| 3 | 53.6 | **48.3-48.7** | 18.7 → 20.6 | 56.0 → **61.9** | 18.9 → 14.3 | 1.55 → 1.15 |

**Single-stream decode gains too, about 1.6 ms a step (+6%).** That is not
yet measured through the server or `ai.service`.

**Measured and dropped:** unpacking each Q4_K weight once and applying it to
every row inside the element loop, which keeps the shared expert's
three-row gain. It cost more than it saved at every row count (29.0 ms at
one row, `shexp.up` 1.25 against 0.72): P11's rule again, a branch inside an
unrolled loop. So a three-row shared expert gives back 0.17 ms of the first
change's gain (0.98 → 1.15).

### A gate this exposed: `TestGraphCheckpointIsThePrefill` fails

**Any change to decode arithmetic makes C4's gate fail**, and the evidence
says the defect predates this change. The restored run matches prefix +
tail for rows 0-10 and moves at **row 11 by 3.5e-4** (logit 0 −2.00677
against −2.00712), deterministically. What is known:

- **The quad kernel fails it, and so does HEAD's kernel with only the
  routed rung changed** (at row 11 again, different digits). HEAD's own
  arithmetic passes at every detour length tried (299-600 tokens, 0 or 12
  steps). So it is not the quad, and HEAD passes by luck.
- **It depends on the detour's length and nothing else found.** The failure
  begins exactly at a 300-token detour, which is the continuation's own
  length and the first detour that writes cell 2899 (pooled block 724, ratio
  4). At 299 or fewer it passes. `LLM_NO_PRERECORD=1` does not change it.
- **Not the pooled table's tail row.** The tail score reads the first
  partial block's pooled row, and an abandoned continuation can leave stale
  keys there. That is real, but writing the fill row back on `Restore` made
  the pooled region byte-identical between the runs, and the logits still
  moved. Reverted.
- Both reference runs differ from each other *and* from the restored run in
  the K/V cache at cells 2896-2911 (by ~4 in value, so masked or stale cells,
  not live keys; the test already notes the first reference is not
  bit-repeatable). Not followed further.

So C4's "bit-identical" claim is unproven on this kernel. The size (3.5e-4 on
one logit, at the 13th row) looks like a summation-order effect, not a wrong
answer, but that is unexplained, not established. **Open.**

'''
s=s.replace('## Next\n', section+'## Next\n',1)
old='''- **What is left in a batched pass:** the MoE is 28.7 of 53.4 ms at three
  rows. Its bytes grow 2.7x with the experts, and `moe.up` still grows 3.1x,
  so a little remains there. Row-aware attention and DeltaNet kernels would
  save up to ~2 ms a row. A batched pass is recorded every step (~1-2 ms of
  host time) rather than replayed like P1c's one-row step.'''
new='''- **`TestGraphCheckpointIsThePrefill` is red** (above): find what a
  300-token detour leaves behind that `Restore` does not undo. Check this
  first, because the gate cannot currently vouch for C4.
- **Re-measure through the server:** single-stream decode (was 34.2 tok/s)
  and C0's mix, now that one-row passes are ~1.6 ms shorter.
- **What is left in a batched pass (48.5 ms at three rows):** `moe.up` is
  14.3 ms and ~3x its one-row cost for 2.7x the experts. The IQ4_NL down
  mode's 36-byte pair records are not 16-aligned and still take scalar
  loads. Row-aware attention and DeltaNet kernels would save up to ~2 ms a
  row. A batched pass is recorded every step (~1-2 ms of host time) rather
  than replayed like P1c's one-row step.'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new)
s=s.rstrip('\n')+'''
- **2026-09-23**: **the MoE GEMV loads once per quad**: Q4_K takes `uvec4`
  header and payload loads, the load is out of the row loop, and the routed
  up mode is v16w4. A three-row pass goes 53.6 → 48.5 ms (61.9 tok/s
  aggregate) and a one-row step 29.2 → 27.6 ms (36.2 tok/s). It exposed
  `TestGraphCheckpointIsThePrefill` as arithmetic-fragile: it fails at row
  11 by 3.5e-4, cause open.
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

Next up in CONCURRENCY.md was "what is left in a batched pass". I made the MoE decode kernel faster, and it now runs a three-row pass in **48.5 ms, down from 53.6**. It also turned up a gate that now fails: C4's checkpoint gate, `TestGraphCheckpointIsThePrefill`. I couldn't find the cause.

**The change** (`shaders/llm_moe_gemv.comp`, `llm/gpu_moe.go`): the expert kernel was limited by how many load instructions it issued, not by memory bandwidth. At three rows, `moe.up` read its weights at about 128 GB/s while `moe.down` reached about 190 on the same tiles. Three changes:
- **Each weight is loaded once for all rows.** Before, the per-row function did its own loads, so a tile with three rows loaded everything three times. The shared expert showed it most: 15.6 / 23.4 / 32.2 µs at 1 / 2 / 3 rows for the same bytes.
- **Q4_K is read 16 bytes at a time.** Each group of four payload words is now two 16-byte loads (header and payload) where it used to be twenty 4-byte loads. The same fix was made to the prefill kernel earlier (P12) and never carried over to this one.
- **The routed up mode moved from `v64w4` to `v16w4`.** I chose it with full 48-layer runs, not the single-layer ladder, which reads the weights from cache (418 GB/s, more than the memory bus can deliver). That ladder once picked `v16w4` wrongly.

Measured with `cmd/llm -batch 1,2,3 -batch-depth 7000` at 48 layers on the shipped banks; "after" is four runs:

| rows | before | after | aggregate |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 29.2 ms | 27.6-27.7 ms | 34.2 → 36.2 tok/s |
| 3 | 53.6 ms | 48.3-48.7 ms | 56.0 → 61.9 tok/s |

Single-stream decode gets about 6% faster too. I haven't measured it through the server yet.

**Correctness:**
- Decode results are no longer bit-identical to before, because the sums are grouped differently. The difference from the prefill kernel is unchanged at rms 2.54e-06.
- Batched rows are still bit-identical to each row run alone.
- `TestGraphLogits` at 48 layers reproduces its numbers to the digit (prefill is untouched).
- The backend `TestLLM*` gates pass, and so does the rest of `go test ./llm/` except the checkpoint gate.

**The failing gate:** a restored checkpoint now differs from a fresh prefill at the last decode row, by 3.5e-4 on one logit, every time.
- **It isn't specific to this kernel.** The old kernel with only the rung changed fails it too. The old code passes because its arithmetic happens not to trip it.
- **It starts exactly when the abandoned continuation reaches 300 tokens.** That is the same length as the real continuation. At 299 tokens or fewer it passes.
- **Two causes ruled out.** It isn't the recorded decode replay. It also isn't a stale row in the indexer's pooled table: I wrote a fix for that, the table came out byte-identical between the runs, and the logits still moved. I reverted that fix.

The size looks like a rounding-order effect rather than a wrong answer, but I haven't shown that. It's written up in CONCURRENCY.md as open and listed first under Next.

Nothing is committed yet; the auto-committer will pick the tree up, failing gate included. Next in the file: find the checkpoint gate's cause, then re-measure decode and the C0 mix through the server.
